title: How to narrate your work
summary_easy: A course in talking about technical work out loud, built entirely from Tanay's own projects. It covers how long each answer should be, how to put numbers into spoken sentences, how to present results that reversed or vanished, and how to handle bugs, not knowing, pushback, AI tool questions and different audiences.
summary_deep: The course is organised around an answer ladder of four nested rungs (10 second hook, 30 second pitch, 2 minute walkthrough, 5 minute deep dive) and two default shapes: Problem, Approach, Result, Lesson for technical questions and STAR for behavioral ones. Number handling rules (result first, one number per sentence, a comparator on every number, the caveat in the same sentence, verbs matched to evidence) are illustrated with Tanay's measured results, from HyperLogLog's 986.9 against 983 exact to JMA's 97.3% uptime beside 46.3% schedule attainment. Hard moments get explicit templates: reversed results (Dr. GRPO), vanished speedups (distributed ViT), bug stories (BEIR truncation, Groundwork's 0.444 threshold), 'I don't know', retrospectives, and a concede, evidence, boundary formula for pushback. Delivery cards cover signposting, branch offers, whiteboarding with rates and failure exits, audience switching, I versus we, honest answers about AI coding tools, transitions, endings without recaps, pacing, filler and stopping. Fifteen drills with model scripts and keypoints turn each technique into practice.

sheet.easy:
## The answer ladder

| Rung | Length | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| Hook | 10 s, about 25 words | What you built or tested plus the surprising result |
| Pitch | 30 s, 60 to 90 words | Hook, why it matters, approach, result with comparator, caveat |
| Walkthrough | 2 min, about 280 words | Problem, setup, approach, result, what broke, next |
| Deep dive | 5 min, 600 to 800 words | Exact claim, controls, mechanism, verification, results, anomaly, deviations |

Each rung starts with the rung above it. Climb one rung at a time, on the part they reacted to.

## Default shapes

- Technical question: Problem, Approach, Result, Lesson.
- 'Tell me about a time': STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result), plus one line of lesson.
- Keep the Situation short and spend half the time on Action.

## Numbers

- Lead with the result.
- One number per sentence. A number and its comparator count as one.
- Every number has a comparator: exact count, published value, matched baseline, target, or naive baseline.
- The caveat goes in the same sentence as the number.
- Verbs match evidence: measured, reproduced, not reproduced here, projected, simulated, upper bound.

## Hard moments

- Reversed result: score each claim, rule out the boring cause, credit what partly held, bound the claim.
- Bug: symptom, ruled out, tell, cause, fix, generalisation.
- I don't know: admit it, known facts, the experiment, a labelled guess.
- Do differently: a decision you made and its cost. Do next: the experiment that most changes confidence.
- Pushback: concede, evidence, boundary.
- AI tools: what you delegated, how you verified, what you caught.

## Delivery

- Signpost the shape, then offer branches ('I can go into A or B') instead of 'does that make sense?'.
- Whiteboard left to right, rates on arrows, exits marked.
- 140 to 160 words a minute, pause before numbers.
- End on a fact, a lesson, or a branch offer. No recap.
- Stop early; they will ask for more.

## Audience

| Audience | Wants | Lead project |
|---|---|---|
| Recruiter | Fit, plain outcome, role words | JMA |
| PM | Decision, user impact, tradeoff | Groundwork precision floor |
| Hiring manager | Ownership and judgement | Distributed ViT diagnosis |
| Staff engineer | Mechanism, alternatives, failure modes | Tool dependency graph |
sheet.deep:
## 1. The ladder in detail

| Rung | Words | Beats | Example opening |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hook | 20 to 30 | object plus surprising result | 'I replicated Dr. GRPO on the paper's own model, data and grader: accuracy held, and both length claims came out reversed.' |
| Pitch | 60 to 90 | hook, why it matters, mechanism, result with comparator, caveat | Wikipedia Edit Stream: HyperLogLog 986.9 against 983 exact, Count-Min barely stressed |
| Walkthrough | 250 to 320 | problem, setup, approach, result, what broke, next | Distributed ViT: 1.96x fp32, 1.15x fp16, 1.92x synthetic, 4 vCPU host |
| Deep dive | 600 to 800 | claim, controls, mechanism, verification, results, anomaly, deviations | Dr. GRPO: two flags, gradient tests, 0.004 nats, reversed lengths, one seed |

Moving up: one rung, on the reacted part, then a branch offer. Moving down: delete setup, then tools, then supporting numbers; keep any caveat that changes the meaning.

## 2. Shapes

**Problem, Approach, Result, Lesson** (technical). Tool dependency graph: agents need opaque handles; schemas resolved to namespaced entities in a bipartite graph; 1,768 of 1,770 typed required inputs have a producer, beside the 65 percent denominator; all eight assertions started out failing.

**STAR** (behavioral). JMA: two lines nobody could compare; project lead of four; definition interviews, sponsor approved document, pipeline; 97.3% uptime beside 46.3% attainment located the constraint upstream. Add the lesson: the finding came from definitions.

## 3. Number bank with comparators and caveats

| Project | Number and comparator | Caveat that travels with it |
|---|---|---|
| Wikipedia Edit Stream | HyperLogLog 986.9 vs 983 exact, inside a 1.6% one sigma bound | Short sessions exercise only the small range path; Count-Min barely collides |
| Order book | 46,892 of 46,892 checksums verified | One venue, 100 levels |
| Earthquake statistics | California b = 0.73, bootstrap [0.66, 0.85] | Pooled b of 0.34 reflects mixed magnitude scales |
| Dr. GRPO | 51.6% vs 51.2% on MATH500, paired [-3.4, +4.0]; Dr. GRPO 99 tokens longer per step [77, 123] | One seed, 100 LoRA steps, 1024 token budget |
| Tool dependency graph | 1,768 of 1,770 typed required inputs have a producer | 65 percent of all required inputs are typed handles |
| Distributed ViT | 98% efficiency fp32 vs 57% fp16; 1.92x with no dataloader | Synthetic 96% is an upper bound |
| ZTF | 27,378 real alerts; dbt 8 models, 21 tests | Archive replay; reference labels are model outputs |
| Groundwork | BM25 recall@5 0.921 vs hybrid 0.853; ECE 0.045; declines 96.2% of unanswerable at a 60% precision floor | Offline extractive reader; hashing embedder |
| BEIR | 6 of 6 cells; DPR 0.260 recovered to the published 0.318 | BM25 is a Python reimplementation, not Anserini |
| JMA | 97.3% uptime vs 46.3% schedule attainment; ~$355K | Projection pending JMA Finance |
| Gravity Spy | 0.89 validation AUC; ECE 0.10 to 0.05 | Agreement with volunteer labels |
| Kp LSTM | 1 hour RMSE 0.738, 45% better than mean baseline | Skill falls with horizon |

## 4. Calibrated verbs

| Verb | Use for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| measured | run artifact on real data | 9,909 real edits in a 297 second run |
| reproduced | match to a published value | BEIR, 6 of 6 |
| not reproduced here | disagreement at smaller scale | Dr. GRPO, one seed |
| projected | a model of the future | JMA ~$355K |
| simulated, synthetic, mock | anything not real | handoff cluster, media-pulse corpus, comms-agent LLM |
| upper bound | best case instrument reading | ViT synthetic input runs |

## 5. Templates for hard moments

**Reversed result.** Score each claim; rule out the boring cause (55 of 500 responses hit the cap in each arm); credit the partial (correct answers 262 vs 399 tokens); bound the claim (one seed, three in the paper).

**Bug.** Symptom (0.260 vs 0.318), ruled out (TAS-B exact), tell (title only 0.261 vs full 0.260), cause (max_seq_length = 100), fix (512 tokens matches the paper), generalisation (chunks longer than the embedder's limit), why it hid (38.2 vs 1.1 judged documents per query).

**Own bug.** The test that caught it and the class of mistake: Groundwork's 0.444 under a 0.5 threshold caught 0 of 60 attacks until a single pattern unit test.

**I don't know.** Admission, known facts, the experiment, labelled guess. GRPO length collapse at steps 55 to 80 is unexplained; truncation similar in both arms.

**Do differently versus next.** JMA: culture metric scoped late, no pipeline tests. ViT next: remove the host ceiling instead of inferring it.

**Pushback.** Concede, evidence, boundary. One seed: concede variance and fp16 nondeterminism; evidence is pairing and the [77, 123] interval; boundary is steps and problems, not seeds. Hybrid: concede it usually wins (BEIR RRF beat both inputs); evidence 6.8 points worse with a hashing embedder; boundary is the flip condition in config.py.

## 6. AI coding tools

1. Delegated: implementation under written house rules in each repo's CLAUDE.md ('Never report a number the code did not measure', 'Never weaken a check to make something pass', 'Never add OnExpiry.ALLOW').
2. Verified: the ViT documentation gate (five unsupported claims on first run), the inverse gradient test, eight hand written graph assertions that all started out failing.
3. Caught: silent defaults (max_seq_length = 100), nearby question APIs (is_bf16_supported), cross module thresholds (0.444 vs 0.5), unfailable tests.

## 7. Whiteboarding

Order: source with rate and format, main path, second plane, orchestration and monitoring, failure exits. Rates to quote: Wikimedia 26 to 36 events a second; Kraken about 142 book updates a second; JMA 31 GB nested JSON to under 5 MB. Groundwork exits: input rail, retrieval empty, context rail, gateway 401/402/429, output rail, calibrated decision.

## 8. Audience map

| Audience | Listens for | Project | Line to land |
|---|---|---|---|
| Recruiter | role words, plain outcome | JMA | 'The automated line was waiting on materials rather than breaking down.' |
| PM | decision and cost | Groundwork | 'At a 60% precision floor it declines 96.2% of unanswerable questions and answers 7.5% of answerable ones.' |
| Hiring manager | judgement without supervision | Distributed ViT | 'One experiment instead of a week tuning NCCL.' |
| Staff engineer | alternatives and failure modes | Tool dependency graph | 'Producers plus consumers instead of producers times consumers.' |

## 9. Transitions

ShopFloor AI to ZTF (closes its three listed gaps); comms-agent to handoff (what happens when the reviewer does not show up); Kp LSTM to Space Weather Nowcast (the live input side of a model trained on clean history).

## 10. Self grading checklist

- Result in the first sentence.
- One number per sentence, each with a comparator.
- Caveat beside its number; verb matches evidence.
- 'I' for your actions, 'we' for shared outcomes.
- A branch offer or a fact at the end; no recap.
- Under two fillers a minute; 140 to 160 words a minute.

narration.prompt: Drill: say the BEIR headline in one sentence with a comparator, then the caveat sentence, then the number if asked.
narration.script: I rebuilt the central BEIR experiment and reproduced six of six published cells, and the one that first disagreed exposed a silent truncation default. The caveat is that my BM25 is a Python reimplementation rather than Anserini, which is the likely source of the only two inexact cells. If you want the number: DPR on SciFact came in at 0.260 against a published 0.318. Raising the encoder's token limit from 100 to 512 brought it to the published value.
keypoints: Headline in one sentence, with 'six of six published' as the comparator
Caveat names the deviation (BM25 not Anserini) and what it costs
Number given only on request, with the published value beside it
No more than one number per sentence
Ends on the fix, without a recap

narration.prompt: Drill: give the Wikipedia Edit Stream hook in 10 seconds. The interviewer says 'go on'. Give the 30 second pitch.
narration.script: Hook: I ran three streaming sketches beside exact counters on Wikipedia's live edit stream, to watch their error bounds hold on real traffic. Pitch, after 'go on': sketches like HyperLogLog promise a bounded error, and people usually take that on faith. Mine run in the browser on the public stream, with an exact counter on the same events. HyperLogLog estimated 986.9 distinct editors against an exact 983. That's well inside its one sigma bound of 1.6%. The honest caveat is that Count-Min barely collides with about a hundred wikis, so its bound is shown but hardly stressed. I can go deeper on the sketch math or on the stream handling.
keypoints: Hook is one sentence with no tool list
Pitch opens by continuing the hook, not restarting
986.9 against 983 exact, then the bound in its own sentence
States the Count-Min caveat unprompted
Ends with a branch offer

narration.prompt: Drill: present the Dr. GRPO replication as a strength in under 45 seconds.
narration.script: I replicated Dr. GRPO on the paper's own model, data and grader, with the two arms differing in exactly two flags. One claim held and two reversed. Accuracy held: 51.6% against 51.2% on MATH500, with a paired interval spanning zero. The length claims went the other way, and Dr. GRPO's wrong answers were longer, not shorter. Truncation doesn't explain it, because each arm hit the cap equally often. Half the mechanism did show up, since GRPO's correct answers got shorter. It's one seed, so I report it as not reproduced here, and I'd want the paper's three seeds before saying refuted.
keypoints: Scores each claim separately
Names the control: two flags differ, everything else paired
Rules out truncation before interpreting
Credits the half of the mechanism that did appear
Bounds the claim: one seed, not reproduced here, never refuted

narration.prompt: Drill: explain the vanished ViT speedup to a hiring manager in 60 seconds, with no jargon beyond 'GPU'.
narration.script: I tested whether splitting training across two GPUs really doubles speed. In standard precision it almost did, 1.96 times faster. Then I switched on a faster number format that makes each GPU roughly twice as quick, and the speedup collapsed to 1.15 times. The obvious suspect was the network between the GPUs, and tuning that could have eaten a week. Instead I ran one experiment that fed the GPUs data straight from memory, skipping the data loading step. With that, two GPUs scaled almost perfectly again. So the machine's CPU, with only four cores, couldn't prepare images fast enough for two fast GPUs. The decision that mattered was running the one experiment that separated the two suspects before tuning anything.
keypoints: Plain words for fp16 and dataloader
Good number, then bad number, each in its own sentence
Names the tempting wrong fix and its cost
One isolating experiment, not trial and error
Ends on the judgement call, not a recap

narration.prompt: Drill: tell the BEIR truncation bug in five beats: symptom, ruled out, tell, cause, generalisation.
narration.script: Symptom: DPR on SciFact scored 0.260 against a published 0.318, too big a gap for rounding. Ruled out: TAS-B had reproduced exactly on both datasets, so the loader and the metrics were fine, which left something about how DPR reads a document. Tell: searching with only the title scored about the same as title plus the full abstract, and that only happens if the body is being discarded. Cause: the sentence-transformers port of the DPR context encoder ships with a 100 token limit, with no warning. Generalisation: any retrieval system whose chunks are longer than its embedder's configured limit has the same silent loss, and the other dataset in my run absorbed the damage so well that it would have hidden the bug on its own.
keypoints: Symptom with the published comparator
Explicitly clears the shared code path using TAS-B
The tell is the title only result, explained
Root cause is a named default with no error or warning
Generalises to production RAG chunking
Mentions why NFCorpus hid it

narration.prompt: Drill: the interviewer says 'One seed is meaningless.' Answer with concede, evidence, boundary.
narration.script: Concede: you're right that one seed can't separate the effect from seed variance, and fp16 on a GPU isn't bit reproducible, so two identical runs drift apart after the first update. Evidence: the comparison is paired, on the same training questions every step and the same eval problems at the end. The per step length gap has a bootstrap interval of 77 to 123 tokens. Boundary: that interval covers steps and problems, not seeds. So I claim not reproduced at this scale, and I'd need the paper's three seeds before calling it anything stronger.
keypoints: Concedes first and specifically (seed variance, fp16 nondeterminism)
Evidence the critic may not know: pairing and the interval
States what the interval does not cover
Neither collapses nor digs in
One number per sentence

narration.prompt: Drill: 'What would you do differently on the JMA project?' Give two decisions and their costs.
narration.script: Two decisions. First, I scoped the Culture and Engagement metric late. The instrument is built and wired into the dashboard, but the first survey slipped past the engagement, so it's the only KPI with no baseline. Next time it goes into the field during Define. Second, I didn't write unit tests for the Python pipeline. It's correct today, but the only thing between an upstream schema change and a silently wrong dashboard is an analyst noticing. A handful of assertions on the schema would have removed that dependency before handover.
keypoints: Names decisions, not circumstances
States the cost of each
Gives the specific fix for each
Keeps it to two items
No defensive framing

narration.prompt: Drill: 'Why did GRPO's response length collapse between steps 55 and 80?' Practise an honest I don't know.
narration.script: I don't know, and my write up lists it as unexplained. What I do know is that truncation during training was similar in both arms, so the token cap isn't the obvious cause. To find out, I'd split per step length into correct and wrong responses across that window, next to reward and format rate. My guess, labelled as a guess, is that GRPO's pressure toward short correct answers dominates once enough answers are correct, because its correct answers did end up much shorter than Dr. GRPO's.
keypoints: Admits it in the first sentence
Gives the known fact that rules out the obvious cause
Names the concrete experiment
Labels the hypothesis as a guess
Grounds the guess in a measured result

narration.prompt: Drill: whiteboard Groundwork's request path in 90 seconds, naming every exit.
narration.script: I'll draw the question coming in on the left. First box, the input rail: injection, jailbreak, length and PII checks, with an exit arrow labelled blocked. Second, retrieval: BM25 by default with optional dense and fusion, and an exit for nothing found. Third, the context rail, which scans retrieved passages for payloads and drops them. It uses only the pattern detector, because the trained classifier fired on every clean encyclopaedia passage. Fourth, the gateway: auth, budget, cache, routing and retries, with exits for bad keys, spent budgets and rate limits, and every call metered. Fifth, the output rail: citations, groundedness and PII egress, with an exit to abstain. Last, the decision box, where calibrated confidence meets a threshold. That exit matters most, because an answer can pass every safety check and still not be confident enough to assert. On the right, the answer leaves with citations and a confidence.
keypoints: Draws left to right in request order
Every stage has a labelled exit
Explains why the context rail uses patterns only
Gateway exits named with status codes
Lands on safe versus confident as the key idea
Talks while drawing, one sentence per box

narration.prompt: Drill: explain the JMA finding twice, first to a PM, then to a staff engineer.
narration.script: To a PM: the automated line looked healthy, running almost all the time, yet it delivered less than half of its weekly plan. A machine that runs constantly and still misses plan is waiting on inputs, so the fix belongs upstream in how materials are kitted, not in the machine. The manual line was covering the gap by running over its own target, which hid the real demand from planning. To a staff engineer: the cell's uptime was 97.3%. Its schedule attainment was 46.3%, and those can't both describe an equipment constraint. The comparison only existed after we fixed one formula per KPI across both lines and I flattened the cell's nested PLC JSON into one typed row per test event. A fishbone put the causes in method, material and measurement: kitting batches sized for the manual line, batched connector subassemblies, and a commissioning era target.
keypoints: PM version has no percentages and states the decision
PM version mentions the hidden demand signal
Engineer version gives each number its own sentence
Engineer version credits the definitions and the pipeline
Engineer version names the fishbone causes

narration.prompt: Drill: transition from the Kp LSTM to Space Weather Nowcast in two sentences, then give the nowcast hook.
narration.script: My Kp forecaster trained on clean hourly history from NASA's OMNI2 dataset, and clean history is the easy part. A model like that would run on live feeds from several spacecraft with gaps, revisions and instrument switches, so I built that input side next. The hook: my dashboard joins nine NOAA feeds on time and propagates the solar wind from L1 to Earth using the active spacecraft's real position. In one run the active spacecraft sat 1.58 million kilometres sunward. The wind it measured was due at Earth 73.5 minutes later.
keypoints: Bridge names the limitation of the first project
Second project framed as the fix for that limitation
Hook is concrete and physical
One number per sentence

narration.prompt: Drill: 'Did you use AI tools to build this?' Answer in under 45 seconds: delegated, verified, caught.
narration.script: Yes, I use Claude Code. My repos keep a working context file with house rules for it, like never report a number the code didn't measure and never weaken a check to make something pass. I verify with checks that don't trust the author. On the ViT project a gate fails the build if any documented number doesn't trace to a run artifact, and it found five unsupported claims the first time. What I catch are errors that read as correct, like a library default that silently truncated documents, or a detector score that sat just under its threshold.
keypoints: Says yes in the first sentence
Delegation is under written rules
Verification is mechanical, not trust
One concrete verification result
Examples of errors that read as correct

narration.prompt: Drill: tie the tool dependency graph to an agent startup's problem and end with a question for them.
narration.script: Agents fail on tool calls for a boring reason: the call needs an argument like a thread id that only an earlier call returns. I built a graph from 1,391 tool schemas that says which tools have to run first and which arguments genuinely have to come from a person. The part that transfers is namespacing: generic names like id collide across services, so name matching wires a mail client to a source control API. How does your agent decide today whether to call another tool or ask the user?
keypoints: Opens with their users' failure, not your project
One number only
Names the transferable mechanism
Ends on a specific question about their system

narration.prompt: Drill: the interviewer says 'we have one minute left'. Compress the distributed ViT walkthrough to 20 seconds.
narration.script: Short version: two GPUs scaled at 98% efficiency in fp32 and dropped to 57% in fp16. One experiment with the dataloader removed brought it back near perfect, so the cause was a 4 core host that couldn't feed faster GPUs, not the network. Scaling efficiency turned out to depend on the ratio of accelerator speed to host speed.
keypoints: Drops setup and tools entirely
Keeps the contrast and the isolating experiment
Ends on the lesson
Does not talk faster to fit

narration.prompt: Drill: give the order book 30 second pitch, then signpost two branches and stop.
narration.script: Every trading system starts from a local copy of the order book, and the classic failure is silent drift: miss one update and every number downstream is quietly wrong. I rebuild Kraken's book in the browser and verify it against the exchange's checksum on every message. In the final run, all 46,892 checksums matched. Only on top of a verified book do I compute order flow imbalance, microprice and realized volatility. I can go into the checksum formatting trap that fails every check if you print one digit wrong, or into the volatility result that went the opposite way from textbook noise.
keypoints: Problem stated in plain words first
Mechanism in one sentence
One result with its comparator (all of them)
Two named branches, then stops

cards.q: What is the answer ladder, and why should every lead project have four rungs ready?
cards.easy: Prepare each lead project at four lengths: a 10 second hook, a 30 second pitch, a 2 minute walkthrough, and a 5 minute deep dive. Answer on the rung the question asks for and move only when the interviewer pulls.
cards.deep: Questions arrive at different zoom levels. 'What's this on your resume?' wants the hook, 'Tell me about a project' wants the pitch, 'Walk me through it' wants the walkthrough, and a technical round's 'How does it work?' wants the deep dive. Each rung contains the one above it: the hook is the first sentence of the pitch, and the pitch is the first paragraph of the walkthrough. That nesting makes movement cheap, because going up means continuing and going down means stopping early. Rough budgets at 140 to 160 spoken words a minute: hook 20 to 30 words, pitch 60 to 90, walkthrough 250 to 320, deep dive 600 to 800. Tanay needs the full ladder only for the six to eight projects that lead for the target role (BEIR, Groundwork, Dr. GRPO, JMA, Gravity Spy, distributed ViT, tool dependency graph, handoff); the rest need a hook and a pitch.
cards.say: For each lead project I keep four lengths ready. The hook for BEIR is one line: I reproduced six of six published cells, and the one that first disagreed exposed a silent truncation bug. If you want more, that sentence becomes the opening of the 30 second version.
evidence: portfolio: 6 of 6 published cells reproduced
portfolio: BADGE: 6 of 6 published cells reproduced / 4 exact / silent truncation bug found and fixed

cards.q: How do I write a 10 second hook for a project?
cards.easy: One sentence: what you built or tested, plus the single most surprising result. No setup and no list of tools.
cards.deep: The hook answers 'what is it, and why should I care' in about 25 words. Template: '[I built / I reproduced / I led] [object], and [the one result that makes an engineer ask a follow up].' The result to pick is the surprising one, which is often a negative result or a bug. Weak: 'I built a Dr. GRPO replication with PyTorch, LoRA and vLLM on Kaggle.' Strong: 'I replicated Dr. GRPO on the paper's own model, data and grader: accuracy held, and both length claims came out reversed.' Tools belong in the walkthrough. Test a hook by whether it invites exactly one follow up ('reversed how?'), because that follow up is answered by the 30 second pitch you already have.
cards.say: I replicated the Dr. GRPO paper on its own model, data and grader. Accuracy held, and both of its length claims came out reversed.
evidence: portfolio: BADGE: 51.6% vs 51.2% on MATH500 / both length claims reversed / 1 seed, 100 steps

cards.q: How do I grow the hook into a 30 second pitch?
cards.easy: Hook, then one sentence each for why it matters, what you did, the result with its comparator, and the caveat. Then stop.
cards.deep: Five sentences, 60 to 90 words. (1) The hook. (2) Why the problem matters, in plain words. (3) The approach, as one mechanism. (4) The result with its comparator. (5) The caveat or the lesson. Wikipedia Edit Stream filled in: streaming sketches come with error bounds that people take on faith; Tanay ran each sketch beside an exact counter on the same live events; HyperLogLog estimated 986.9 distinct editors against an exact 983, inside its one sigma bound of 1.6%; Count-Min barely collides with about 100 wikis in 1,024 columns, so its bound is shown but hardly stressed. The caveat sentence separates a pitch from marketing, and it answers the sharpest follow up before anyone asks it.
cards.say: Streaming sketches come with error bounds that people usually take on faith. I ran three of them beside exact counters on Wikipedia's live edit stream, in the browser. HyperLogLog estimated 986.9 distinct editors against an exact 983. That's inside its one sigma bound of 1.6%. The honest caveat is that Count-Min barely collides at this volume, so its bound is shown but hardly stressed.
evidence: portfolio: HyperLogLog estimated 986.9 distinct editors against an exact 983, an error of +0.4% against a one sigma bound of 1.6%.
portfolio: Count-Min barely collides here. About 100 wikis in 1,024 columns rarely share a cell, so the bound is shown but hardly stressed.
portfolio: I wanted to watch those promises hold on real traffic instead of taking them on faith

cards.q: What goes into the 2 minute walkthrough?
cards.easy: The pitch, expanded into six beats: problem, setup, approach, result, what broke, and what you would do next. About 280 words.
cards.deep: Roughly 20 seconds per beat. Problem: why anyone should care. Setup: data or hardware, with one quirk. Approach: the one or two mechanisms that matter, named. Result: the headline number with its comparator, then at most one supporting number. What broke: the bug or the wrong prediction, usually the most memorable part. Next: one concrete step. Distributed ViT filled in: distributed speedups are usually unverifiable; 2x Tesla T4 with a gradient equivalence test before any timing; DDP scaled 1.96x in fp32; the identical config in fp16 fell to 1.15x; a synthetic input mode with no dataloader scaled at 1.92x, which cleared the collective and pointed at a 4 vCPU host; next is confirming that by removing the ceiling instead of inferring it. Drop tool names unless they carry meaning.
cards.say: This project tests a distributed training speedup instead of just claiming one. Before timing anything, I checked that two ranks compute the same gradient as one rank with double the batch. On two T4s in fp32, DDP scaled at 1.96x. Then I turned on mixed precision and the same setup fell to 1.15x. I ran a synthetic input mode with no dataloader, and the collective scaled at 1.92x. So communication was fine, and the artifacts showed a host with 4 CPU cores that couldn't feed two faster GPUs. Next I'd confirm that on a machine with more cores instead of inferring it.
evidence: portfolio: 2x Tesla T4, NCCL
portfolio: DDP in fp32: 1.96x at 98% efficiency
portfolio: identical config in fp16: 1.15x at 57%
portfolio: With no dataloader the same configuration scales at 1.92x, 96% efficiency.
portfolio: The artifacts record cpu_cores: 4.
repo:distributed-vit-cifar10/CLAUDE.md: 1. Confirm the diagnosis by removing the ceiling rather than inferring it.

cards.q: What does a 5 minute deep dive add that the walkthrough does not?
cards.easy: Mechanism and evidence: the exact claim, what was held fixed, the one equation or design choice that matters, how correctness was checked, and how far the result generalises.
cards.deep: Seven parts, with a pause after each so the interviewer can steer. (1) Restate the claim precisely. (2) Setup and what was held fixed. (3) The mechanism at whiteboard level, with the one equation that matters. (4) How correctness was verified before results were trusted. (5) Results with intervals. (6) The anomaly and what it taught. (7) Deviations from the reference. cards.q: What is Problem, Approach, Result, Lesson, and why is it the default shape for a technical project?
cards.easy: Problem: what was broken or unknown. Approach: what you did and why that way. Result: what happened, with a number and comparator. Lesson: what you know now that you did not before.
cards.deep: The four beats match how engineers judge work: was the problem real, was the approach sound against the alternatives, is the result measured against something, and did the person learn something transferable. Lesson is the beat most candidates skip and the one that shows judgement. Tool dependency graph filled in. Problem: agents fail tool calls when they need an opaque handle such as thread_id that only an earlier call returns. Approach: derive which tools must run first from 1,391 tool schemas, resolving handles to namespaced entities and drawing a bipartite graph of tools and entities. Result: 1,768 of 1,770 typed required inputs have a producer, reported beside the honest denominator that 65 percent of all required inputs are typed handles. Lesson: all eight hand written assertions started out failing, and the four real bugs they exposed were invisible from reading the code. In a walkthrough, keep each beat to two or three sentences.

The lesson was that all eight of my assertions started out failing, and none of the four real bugs were visible from reading the code.

cards.q: How do I lead with the result instead of building up to it?
cards.easy: Say what happened in the first sentence, then explain how you got there. The listener can only follow reasoning if they know where it ends.
cards.deep: Chronological telling ('first I downloaded the data, then...') makes the listener hold every detail without knowing which ones matter. Result first gives a frame, and every later sentence becomes evidence for a claim already heard. Technique: write the last sentence of the story, move it to the front, and cut whatever does not support it. Groundwork, chronological: 'I built a RAG system on SQuAD v2, added BM25, then a dense retriever, then fused them...'. Groundwork, result first: 'My own evaluation removed hybrid retrieval: fusion was 6.8 points of recall@5 worse than BM25 alone, because the hashing embedder has no semantic generalisation.' Leading with the result also forces you to know what the result is, which is most of the preparation.

cards.q: What if my result is small or negative? Should I still lead with it?
cards.easy: Yes. State it plainly and first, then say what it is evidence of. A negative result stated first sounds confident; one revealed at the end sounds like a confession.
cards.deep: Burying a weak result invites the interviewer to discover it, which costs more trust than stating it. State it, attach the comparator, and follow at once with what it taught. cards.q: Why does every number need a comparator, and which comparators are strongest?

cards.q: How do I present a result that did not replicate?
cards.easy: Score each claim separately, show you ruled out the boring explanation, say what partly reproduced, and bound the claim. Say 'not reproduced here', never 'refuted', unless you matched the original's scale.

(3) Say what partly reproduced: GRPO's correct answers did get shorter, 262 against 399 tokens. (4) Bound it: one seed against the paper's three, 100 LoRA steps, a 1024 token budget, which is why it reads as not reproduced here. Framed this way the reversal is a strength, because it shows you can disagree with a paper without overstating.

cards.q: How do I present a speedup that vanished?
cards.easy: Make the vanishing the finding. Give the good number, the bad number, the two suspects, and the experiment that separated them.
cards.deep: An explained regression is worth more than a reported speedup, because explaining it takes a controlled experiment. Structure for distributed ViT: (1) the matched baseline rule, so the drop is real: a rank scaling baseline differs from its run only in rank count; (2) the drop: 1.96x at 98% in fp32, 1.15x at 57% in fp16; (3) two named suspects, the NCCL all reduce and the input pipeline; (4) the isolating experiment, a synthetic input mode with no dataloader, which scaled at 1.92x; (5) the confirming clues, cpu_cores: 4 in the artifacts, and 8 workers per rank doing worse than 2 (3,996 against 4,073 img/s); (6) the general lesson, that optimising the accelerator moved the bottleneck to the host. cards.q: Which verbs should I use for the strength of a claim?
cards.easy: Match the verb to the evidence: measured, reproduced, not reproduced here, projected, on synthetic data, upper bound. Never upgrade a projection to a saving or a single seed to a refutation.
cards.deep: A small fixed vocabulary keeps you honest under pressure. 'Measured' for a number from a run on real data. 'Reproduced' for a match to a published value (BEIR: 6 of 6 cells, 4 exact to three decimals). 'Not reproduced here' for a disagreement at smaller scale (Dr. GRPO, one seed, 100 steps). 'Projected' or 'sized opportunity' for a model of the future (JMA's ~$355K). 'On synthetic data', 'with a mock model' or 'simulated' for anything not real (media-pulse's corpus, comms-agent's mock LLM, handoff's dataclass cluster). 'Upper bound' for a best case instrument reading (the ViT synthetic runs index a small pool, so their 96% bounds what fixing the input path could achieve). Interviewers at research minded startups listen for these verbs, and one overclaim discounts everything else.

cards.q: What is signposting, and how do I do it?
cards.easy: Tell the listener the shape of the answer before you give it ('two parts: the model and the warehouse'), then use the signposts as you go.

cards.q: How do I whiteboard a pipeline?
cards.easy: Draw left to right: source, ingest, transform, store, serve, monitor. Label every arrow with a format and a rate. Then mark where it can break.

First the source box, with format and volume (ZTF: Avro packets over Kafka, a real night of 27,378 alerts replayed through a Dockerized broker). Second the main path: deserialize, score, land in the warehouse. Third the second plane: dbt staging, intermediate lightcurves, marts. Fourth, orchestration and monitoring around the edges: the Airflow DAG, a PSI drift monitor on the prediction distribution, CI running a dbt build on every push. Fifth, failure marks: where data can be late, wrong or duplicated, and what catches it (source freshness checks, the 21 dbt tests). Say one sentence per box while drawing, never draw silently for more than ten seconds, and leave room on the right for the '100x' question.

The places it breaks are late data and schema drift, so freshness checks and tests sit there.

cards.q: How do I show on a whiteboard where a system can stop or fail?
cards.easy: Draw the happy path, then an exit arrow at every stage that can stop the request, labelled with the reason. It shows you designed for failure.

The gateway can return 401, 402 or 429 on auth, budget or rate. The output rail can abstain on citations, groundedness or PII egress. The decision stage can abstain when calibrated confidence is under threshold. The talking point is the last exit: an answer can pass every safety check and still be one the system should not assert, and separating safe from confident lets a product hedge instead of choosing between bluffing and refusing. Put the measured number on the exit that has one: at a 60% precision floor the system correctly declines 96.2% of unanswerable questions.

cards.q: How fast should I talk, and how do I control pace under nerves?
cards.easy: Slower than feels natural, around 140 to 160 words a minute, with a short pause before every number and after every result.
cards.deep: Nerves push most speakers past 180 words a minute, where numbers blur together. Short sentences give natural places to breathe. Calibrate with a recording: the 30 second pitch should take 25 to 35 seconds, and if a 75 word pitch takes 20 you are rushing. On video calls add a beat after finishing, because audio lag invites collisions. Measured speech reads as confidence.

cards.q: How do I cut filler words like 'um', 'like', 'basically' and 'so yeah'?
